nameStory: The squirrel tree frog gets its name from its quick, agile movements as it scampers through branches and vegetation, much like a tiny squirrel navigating the treetops. These little acrobats are surprisingly nimble climbers, using their sticky toe pads to dart from leaf to leaf with squirrel-like energy and grace.
description: The squirrel tree frog is a tiny amphibian, reaching only about 1.5 inches long as an adult - small enough to sit comfortably on a quarter. These miniature climbers are typically bright green, closely resembling their cousin the American green tree frog, though they can also appear in shades of yellow or brown. They're naturally found in the southeastern United States but have been spotted just once in New England, making them an extremely rare visitor to our region.

idTips.label: Size
idTips.description: Remarkably small at just 1.5 inches long - about the size of your thumbnail. This tiny stature immediately sets it apart from most other tree frogs you'll encounter.

idTips.label: Color/Pattern
idTips.description: Usually bright green like a fresh spring leaf, but can shift to yellow or brown. Males often sport a bold dark stripe along their sides that looks like it was painted with a marker.

idTips.label: Skin
idTips.description: Smooth, slightly moist skin that feels cool and soft to the touch, like damp silk. The surface has a subtle sheen that catches light beautifully.

idTips.label: Eyes
idTips.description: Large, prominent eyes that seem oversized for their tiny head, giving them an alert, curious expression as they scan for insects.

idTips.label: Habitat
idTips.description: Found clinging to vegetation near water sources, often on broad leaves or smooth bark where their toe pads can get the best grip.

habitat: In New England, this would be an extraordinary find, as squirrel tree frogs naturally live much further south. If encountered, it would likely be near wetlands, ponds, or streams where it could find the insects and moisture it needs. Look for them on smooth-barked trees, large-leafed plants, or garden vegetation close to water sources.

seasonality.spring: Extremely unlikely to be seen in New England during spring, as this is far outside their natural range. Any sighting would be remarkable and worth reporting to local naturalists.
seasonality.summer: If present at all, summer would be the most likely time to spot one, when they'd be most active hunting insects on warm, humid evenings near water.
seasonality.fall: Activity would slow dramatically in fall as temperatures drop, making any potential sighting even more unlikely in our cooler New England climate.
seasonality.winter: Cannot survive New England winters outdoors, so any previous visitors would have either died or moved indoors to heated spaces.

funFact: Despite being called a 'tree' frog, squirrel tree frogs are actually excellent swimmers and often dive underwater to escape predators, staying submerged for several minutes while holding their breath - a talent most people never get to witness!
confusionNotes: Most likely to be confused with a very young green tree frog, but squirrel tree frogs are much smaller and often have that distinctive dark side stripe on males. Remember: if it's truly tiny and has racing stripes, think squirrel frog!
contextualKnowledge: With only one recorded observation in New England, this species represents either an accidental introduction (perhaps in shipped plants) or climate-driven range expansion. Any sighting should be documented with photos and reported to local wildlife authorities, as it would be scientifically significant.
compareHints: Compared to its New England relatives, the squirrel tree frog is much smaller than both gray treefrogs and green treefrogs. Gray treefrogs have rougher, warty skin and are significantly larger, while green treefrogs in New England are also bigger and lack the prominent side stripes often seen on male squirrel tree frogs. The tiny size is really the key difference - if you can cover it completely with a quarter, you might have found our region's rarest tree frog.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Unlike the Green Treefrog which maintains a consistent bright green color, Gray Treefrogs are the masters of camouflage with their color-changing abilities.
Green Treefrogs differ from their close relative the Gray Treefrog by maintaining bright green coloration and having a more streamlined body shape.
